title: Counting the compute
objectives: Derive the 6ND rule for training compute and apply it to real models.

screens.title: One token through the tiny GPT
screens.prose: Multiplying a vector by a weight matrix costs one multiply and one add per weight. Almost every parameter of a GPT is a matrix weight that each token meets once in the forward pass. Here $N$ counts every parameter. Kaplan et al. leave out the embedding tables, which a token looks up rather than multiplies: that leaves 14,913 of the tiny GPT's 18,017.
screens.question: About how many floating-point operations does one token's forward pass take?

hints.text: Each weight: one multiply, one add.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Two operations per weight.

byKey.one: That counts one operation per weight. A multiply and an add make two.
byKey.six: That is the training cost, forward and backward.

explain.text: A forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token: 36,034 for the tiny GPT. Attention scores add a little more, which we count later.

screens.title: Forward and backward
screens.prose: The backward pass needs two products per weight matrix: one for the input's gradient and one for the weight's. So it costs about twice the forward pass. Slide through four training runs.
screens.question: What share of training compute is the backward pass?

options.why: The backward pass does two products per weight to the forward pass's one.
It is twice the forward pass, not dozens of times.

feedback.correct: $4N$ of $6N$ per token: two thirds, in every run.

explain.text: Forward $2N$, backward $4N$: training costs about $6N$ FLOPs per token, so $6ND$ for $D$ tokens. The split is the same at every size.

screens.title: GPT-3's compute
screens.prose: The rule **$C \approx 6ND$**: $N$ parameters trained on $D$ tokens. GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters and was trained on 300 billion tokens.
screens.question: What is $C$, in units of $10^{23}$ FLOPs? Give 2 decimal places.

byKey.fwd: That is $2ND$, the forward pass only.

explain.text: $6ND = 3.15 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs. The GPT-3 paper's table gives $3.14 \times 10^{23}$; the rule is an approximation, and we quote 3.15 from it.

screens.title: Chinchilla's compute
screens.prose: Chinchilla has 70 billion parameters and was trained on 1.4 trillion tokens.
screens.question: How many training tokens did Chinchilla see per parameter?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the tokens by the parameters.

byKey.inv: You divided the parameters by the tokens.

explain.text: Chinchilla: 20 tokens per parameter and $5.88 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs, against GPT-3's 1.7 tokens per parameter. Level 4 ends on why.

screens.title: The tiny GPT's run
screens.prose: The supplied tiny GPT trained for 5,000 steps of 16 windows of 32 characters: 2,560,000 tokens, so $6ND = 2.77 \times 10^{11}$ FLOPs. The browser's matrix products ran at about 2.1 GFLOP/s in the timing spike.
screens.question: How many seconds would the run take if every FLOP ran at 2.1 GFLOP/s? Give 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Divide FLOPs by FLOPs per second.

feedback.correct: $2.77 \times 10^{11} / 2.1 \times 10^9 \approx 131.8$ s. Measured, a step takes 56 ms in the browser, so the run would take 280 s.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the FLOPs by the speed.

byKey.min: That is minutes. The question asks for seconds.

explain.text: 131.8 s at matmul speed, but the measured 56 ms a step makes 280 s: an effective 0.99 GFLOP/s. Small matrices and Python overhead waste most of the peak.

screens.title: The attention term
screens.prose: $2N$ counts the weights. Attention also compares each token with every earlier one: about $2LTd$ more FLOPs per token forward (Kaplan et al. 2020). For GPT-2 small, $L = 12$, $T = 1{,}024$, $d = 768$; its blocks hold 85,054,464 weights.
screens.question: What is $2LTd$ as a share of $2N$ for the blocks? Give a percentage to one decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide $2LTd$ by twice the block weights.

byKey.total: You used the whole model, embeddings included. Compare with the blocks.

explain.text: At a context of 1,024 the attention term adds 11.1%. It grows with $T$, so long contexts change the picture.

screens.title: Write the cost functions
screens.prose: Write `train_flops(N, D)`, `attention_flops(L, T, d)` (the $2LTd$ forward term per token) and `days_to_train(flops, flops_per_s, utilisation)`, where utilisation is the fraction of the peak rate a run achieves.
screens.question: Write the three functions.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests: GPT-3 and the tiny GPT's training FLOPs, GPT-2 small's attention term, GPT-3 on 1,000 GPUs at 40%, one day at full use, and a toy attention term. Values within $10^{-9}$ (relative).

mutants.symptom: Counts only the forward pass, 2ND, which is inference.
Ignores utilisation, as if every FLOP ran at the peak rate.
Divides by the seconds in an hour, giving hours.
Squares the context, the cost of a whole sequence, not of one token.

hints.text: Divide by the achieved rate, `flops_per_s * utilisation`.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 uses 40% utilisation and days, not hours.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is one token's attention across the context: $2LTd$, with $T$ once, not squared.

explain.text: Compute, then time at the rate actually achieved. Utilisation of 30% to 50% of peak is typical for large training runs.

screens.title: Training is not inference
screens.prose: A colleague budgets GPT-3's training as $2ND$: "two FLOPs per parameter per token".
screens.question: What is wrong with the estimate?

options.text: $2ND$ is the forward pass only; training adds the backward pass, $4ND$
Nothing: two FLOPs per weight is right
options.why: Right for a forward pass, which is what serving a model costs; training also runs backward.
The backward pass costs twice the forward pass, so $6ND$ in all.

options.text: It leaves out attention, which triples the cost
options.why: Attention adds about 1.4% at GPT-3's context, not 200%.

hints.text: What does each FLOP count cover?

feedback.correct: $2ND$ is inference. Training is forward plus backward, $6ND$: three times as much.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does the backward pass cost?

byKey.ok: That is the trap: $2N$ per token is the cost of using the model. Training costs three times as much.

explain.text: Generating a token costs about $2N$ FLOPs; training on it costs about $6N$. A budget built on $2ND$ is short by a factor of 3.

screens.title: When attention dominates
screens.prose: The weights cost about $24Ld^2$ FLOPs per token forward ($2N$ with $N \approx 12Ld^2$), and attention $2LTd$. The two are equal when $T = 12d$.

columns: Context where attention equals the weights

screens.question: For width 768, at what context length does the attention term equal the weight term?

byKey.d: That is $T = d$. Solve the equation for $T$.
byKey.sq: That is $d^2$. Divide both sides by $2Ld$.

explain.text: Below 9,216 tokens of context, GPT-2 small's weights dominate its compute; above it, attention does. Long-context models need the attention term in their budget.

screens.title: Days on a cluster
screens.prose: Train GPT-3 ($3.15 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs) on 1,000 GPUs, each with a peak of 312 TFLOP/s in bf16, at 40% utilisation.
screens.question: How many days does it take? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the achieved rate, then by the seconds in a day.

explain.text: About 29.2 days on 1,000 GPUs. At full utilisation it would be 11.7; real runs rarely pass half the peak.

screens.title: The compute rule
screens.prose:
Training compute:
$$C \approx 6ND \quad (2N \text{ forward} + 4N \text{ backward per token})$$
plus about $6LTd$ per token for attention when the context is long. Time is $C$ over the achieved rate.
screens.question: Double both $N$ and $D$. By how much does $C$ grow?

options.why: $C$ is a product of both, so each doubling counts.
The 6 is a constant; it does not change.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply both factors by 2.

explain.text: Compute is bilinear in model size and data. A model twice as large on twice the data costs 4 times as much.

screens.title: Budgeting in pounds
screens.prose: The GPT-3 run above takes about 29.2 days on 1,000 GPUs. A cloud provider charges £1.50 per GPU-hour.
screens.question: What does the run cost in pounds, to the nearest thousand?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count GPU-hours, then multiply by the rate.

byKey.day: You charged per GPU-day. The rate is per hour.
byKey.one: You counted one GPU. There are 1,000.

explain.text: About 701,122 GPU-hours, so about £1,052,000, before failed runs, experiments and storage. The same arithmetic prices any research cluster.

ideas: A forward pass costs about $2N$ FLOPs per token and the backward pass $4N$, so training costs $C \approx 6ND$; inference costs $2N$ per token.
GPT-3: $3.15 \times 10^{23}$ FLOPs; Chinchilla: $5.88 \times 10^{23}$ at 20 tokens per parameter; the tiny GPT: $2.77 \times 10^{11}$.
Attention adds about $2LTd$ per token forward and dominates once $T > 12d$; days are $C$ over the achieved rate.
summary.trap: Budgeting training with $2ND$, the cost of inference.

quiz.question: A model of $10^9$ parameters is trained on $2 \times 10^{10}$ tokens. What is its training compute, in units of $10^{20}$ FLOPs?
Generating one token with a 70-billion-parameter model costs about how many FLOPs?

options.why: That includes a backward pass, which generation does not run.
Each weight costs a multiply and an add.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which passes does generation run?

explain.text: Generation runs the forward pass only: $2 \times 7 \times 10^{10}$ FLOPs per token.

quiz.question: A run needs 10 days at full utilisation. How long at 25% utilisation?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the utilisation.

explain.text: Achieving a quarter of the peak makes the run 4 times longer: 40 days.
